stage_name: Live HIL round for S6 #12/FD-17 (certificate rotation) on real ESP32-C6 hardware -- did not reach the certificate-rotation route itself, but found and fixed four real, hardware-only-discoverable defects blocking a stable boot with real Wi-Fi connectivity. The route exercise itself (POST /api/v1/security/certificates/operations against a live device) remains open, blocked by a separate, unresolved Wi-Fi station auth issue on the one board with Flash Encryption already provisioned.
note_on_commits: No new commit created; commits are only made on explicit user request. Builds on the same uncommitted tree as S6-cert-rotation-state-and-route-completion.json.
sequencing_note: User authorized live HIL for cert-rotation ('Так, робимо HIL зараз'). The route was never reached: real hardware crashed before WebServer::start() on every attempt, for reasons unrelated to cert-rotation's own code. Each bug below was found by booting real hardware, diagnosed with real evidence (UART core dumps, addr2line against the real build ELF, real heap diagnostics), fixed, and re-verified on real hardware -- the same methodology this project's memory documents as its standing verification bar.

real_defects_found_and_fixed.defect: Stack overflow / silent LP-RAM fallback in ServiceRuntime::start()'s task creation.
real_defects_found_and_fixed.how_found: Real 'Guru Meditation Error: Stack protection fault' on first-ever real hardware boot with a connected Wi-Fi network. UART core dump (CONFIG_ESP_COREDUMP_ENABLE_TO_UART, base64-framed ELF stripped of ESP-IDF's own length/checksum header before the real \x7fELF magic) decoded via `idf.py coredump-info` showed task "service_runtime" with stack bounds landing in 0x50000000 (LP-RAM/RTC memory, ~15KB, meant for ULP code).
real_defects_found_and_fixed.root_cause: Confirmed by reading ESP-IDF's own real components/heap/port/esp32c6/memory_layout.c: on ESP32-C6, MALLOC_CAP_INTERNAL|MALLOC_CAP_8BIT alone does not exclude LP-RAM -- RTCRAM's own medium-priority capability set includes exactly those two flags, so plain xTaskCreate()'s default allocator silently falls through to LP-RAM once the real SRAM pool's high-priority region can't satisfy a request, reporting pdPASS either way.
real_defects_found_and_fixed.fix: New components/app_hal/hal_memory.c/.h: hal_alloc_internal_sram()/hal_free_internal_sram(), using MALLOC_CAP_INTERNAL|MALLOC_CAP_8BIT|MALLOC_CAP_DMA -- MALLOC_CAP_DMA is the one capability present only in real SRAM's own high-priority set, never in RTCRAM's sets at any tier. Lives in app_hal (not service) because INV-H002 forbids the service layer from calling malloc-family functions directly -- same relocation precedent hal_tls_certificate_validator.h already established. service_runtime.cpp's ServiceRuntime::start() now uses xTaskCreateStatic() via a new create_task_pinned_to_internal_stack() helper for all 3 tasks it creates, instead of plain xTaskCreate().
real_defects_found_and_fixed.secondary_fix: Even with the correct capability flags, g_runtime.start() still failed closed: real heap diagnostics showed initialize_hal_adapter() (Wi-Fi driver init alone, no connection yet) consumes roughly 65KB of the ~77-148KB available at app_main() start (the exact figure depends on Flash Encryption / production profile -- see Bug F below), leaving too little DMA-capable free where g_runtime.start() originally ran (after Wi-Fi connect/mDNS). Fixed by reordering app_main.cpp to call g_runtime.start() immediately after initialize_hal_adapter(), before the Wi-Fi credential bootstrap / autoconnect_from_saved_credentials() block -- safe because config_manager_.load() already runs in ServiceRuntime's own constructor, well before app_main() starts, so start()'s task-creation has no real ordering dependency on Wi-Fi.
real_defects_found_and_fixed.tertiary_fix: Even after reordering, scan_worker_task/rcp_worker_task (4608/4096 bytes) still didn't always fit in the remaining budget. Made their creation non-fatal (log a warning, continue boot, leave the handle null) rather than failing the whole boot -- matches this project's own established graceful-degradation posture already applied to MQTT/Matter/Zigbee when a capability/resource isn't available.
real_defects_found_and_fixed.verified: Real hardware: "Service runtime task started" now appears reliably on every boot cycle across all subsequent HIL rounds this session, on every board and every profile tested.

real_defects_found_and_fixed.defect: A second, different stack overflow in CoreRegistry::snapshot_copy()'s own by-value local, unreachable until the very first time this project's code ever received a real Wi-Fi 'connected' event on hardware.
real_defects_found_and_fixed.how_found: Real 'Stack protection fault' immediately after 'Auto-connect: Wi-Fi connect requested'. This time idf.py coredump-info itself failed (construct.core.StreamError -- a declared program-header filesz exceeded the actually-captured bytes, reproduced identically across two independently captured coredumps, ruling out simple transmission corruption -- most likely the on-device coredump writer itself truncating under heap pressure at panic time). Fallback: resolved the panic's own printed PC/RA registers directly via `riscv32-esp-elf-addr2line -pfiaC` against the real build ELF.
real_defects_found_and_fixed.root_cause: PC = core::CoreRegistry::snapshot_copy() (components/core/core_registry.cpp:50), RA = service::StatePersistenceCoordinator::persist_current_core_state() (components/service/state_persistence_coordinator.cpp:84). persist_current_core_state() already had a code comment documenting this exact bug class and claiming a fix (a `static` local instead of a stack-local) -- but explicitly scoped it to that one function, leaving CoreRegistry::snapshot_copy() itself (a shared public API with many other, host-test-only callers) with its own un-`static`-able local `const CoreState copy = *ref.state;` (CoreState is roughly 2.5KB with kMaxDevices=64 -- cannot safely be `static` since CoreRegistry supports concurrent callers via its own SnapshotRef pin/release mechanism). Real hardware proved that 'not a concern' assumption wrong for at least this one real caller/call-depth. Stack bounds this time were correctly in real SRAM (0x40868xxx), not LP-RAM -- confirming Bug A's fix held; this was purely a budget shortfall, not a wrong-memory-region bug.
real_defects_found_and_fixed.fix: kRuntimeTaskStackSize (service_runtime.cpp) raised from 9216 to 16384 bytes, chosen over redesigning CoreRegistry::snapshot_copy()'s by-value-return API (a user decision via AskUserQuestion -- lower risk, matches Bug A's own established stack-bump pattern rather than a wider API change touching every other caller).
real_defects_found_and_fixed.verified: Real hardware: 2 full boot cycles including a real 'wifi:connected with...' event, zero panics, boot proceeded to 'Auto-connect started from saved credentials' -- the first time this project's code has ever processed a real Wi-Fi connected event on hardware without crashing.

real_defects_found_and_fixed.defect: hal_zigbee.c's zigbee_main task -- same LP-RAM-fallback class as Bug A, never covered by Bug A's own fix (a different component: app_hal, not service).
real_defects_found_and_fixed.how_found: After Bug D's fix, boot proceeded further than ever before and hit a third crash: 'No memory for I/O buffer' -> 'Zigbee stack assertion failed common/zb_memconfig.c:166' -> abort(), with the faulting task's SP in the 0x50000000 (LP-RAM) range.
real_defects_found_and_fixed.root_cause: hal_zigbee.c's hal_zigbee_init() created the 'zigbee_main' task via plain xTaskCreate() (8192-byte stack) -- Bug A's fix only ever touched service_runtime.cpp's own 3 tasks, never this one. Same mechanism as Bug A: the task's own stack silently fell back to the ~15KB LP-RAM pool, and once there, starved whatever internal 'I/O buffer' allocation the vendored esp-zigbee-lib tries to carve from that same capability-matched pool right after.
real_defects_found_and_fixed.fix: Same hal_alloc_internal_sram() + xTaskCreateStatic() pattern as Bug A, applied to zigbee_main in hal_zigbee.c (already in app_hal, no arch-invariant relocation needed -- hal_memory.h just #include'd directly). User explicitly flagged this as outside the current HIL round's own scope (Zigbee, not Wi-Fi/TLS) before authorizing the fix via AskUserQuestion.
real_defects_found_and_fixed.verified: Real hardware, with an important honest twist: after the fix, Zigbee no longer aborts -- but hal_alloc_internal_sram(8192) can genuinely, honestly fail (real internal-SRAM exhaustion by ~17s into boot, after Wi-Fi+MQTT+web-server have all claimed their share) and the fail-closed path logs 'Failed to allocate Zigbee stack task stack (internal SRAM)' -> 'Deferred Zigbee start... started=no' -- no crash, clean graceful degradation matching this project's established posture for unavailable capabilities. Captured a full 40+ second boot window with zero crashes end to end, including the web server starting -- the first time this whole HIL investigation reached a fully stable, web-server-up device.

real_defects_found_and_fixed.defect: Bug D's own fix (kRuntimeTaskStackSize=16384) regressed the PRODUCTION + Flash-Encryption-Development profile -- service_runtime failed to start at all there.
real_defects_found_and_fixed.how_found: Real hardware: on the production/flash-encryption-dev profile, only ~12.3KB DMA-capable heap was free at the same boot point where the non-production/non-encrypted board had ~80KB free (free=77936 at app_main() start on the production/flash-enc profile vs. free=147392 on the identical code without it -- Flash Encryption + nvs_sec_provider overhead roughly halves the heap budget available on this device at that point in boot). 16384 exceeded the largest available contiguous block (12288), so xTaskCreateStatic() correctly failed closed -- but this meant service_runtime never started at all, a worse outcome than Bug D's original overflow.
real_defects_found_and_fixed.root_cause: A single fixed stack-size constant cannot simultaneously satisfy Bug D's real ~10048-byte peak need and the production profile's own, much tighter heap ceiling -- 16384 was tuned only against the non-production board's own numbers.
real_defects_found_and_fixed.fix: kRuntimeTaskStackSize re-tuned to 11264 bytes -- the one value real HIL confirmed fits both profiles measured on this hardware (roughly 1KB margin under the tighter production ceiling, roughly 1.2KB margin over the measured Bug D peak need).
real_defects_found_and_fixed.verified: Real hardware, production + Flash-Encryption-Development profile: 'Service runtime task started' now appears reliably again. Re-verified 16/16 boot cycles with no task-creation failures.

modified: components/app_hal/hal_zigbee.c (zigbee_main task creation switched to xTaskCreateStatic()+hal_alloc_internal_sram(), Bug E)

components/service/service_runtime.cpp (create_task_pinned_to_internal_stack() helper; all 3 task creations switched to xTaskCreateStatic(); scan-worker/RCP-worker creation made non-fatal; kRuntimeTaskStackSize tuned 9216 -> 16384 -> 11264 across Bugs A/D/F)

main/app_main.cpp (g_runtime.start() call block moved to immediately after initialize_hal_adapter(), before the Wi-Fi autoconnect/AP-start block -- Bug A's real, permanent fix; all temporary [HIL-DIAG] diagnostics and the one-time real-credential Wi-Fi bootstrap block used to drive this HIL round removed afterward, along with their now-unused esp_heap_caps.h/esp_system.h/hal_nvs.h includes)

tests_and_checks.result: Zero crashes across 40+ second window: Wi-Fi station connects, autoconnect completes, development HTTP web server starts, Zigbee gracefully defers (honest internal-SRAM shortage, not a crash). First fully stable boot this whole HIL investigation reached.

tests_and_checks.check: Real hardware, first ESP32-C6 board (Flash Encryption Development mode, production profile, the board originally targeted for the cert-rotation route itself), full boot capture
tests_and_checks.result: service_runtime starts reliably (Bug F fix verified, 16/16 cycles). Wi-Fi station connect itself still fails 100% of the time (see honest_scope_boundary) -- unrelated to any of the four bugs in this file, and NOT fixed this round.

honest_scope_boundary: The ORIGINAL goal of this HIL round -- exercising the real POST /api/v1/security/certificates/operations route against a live, cleanly-booted device -- was NOT reached. All four bugs above were found and fixed along the way, but a separate, still-unresolved Wi-Fi station connectivity issue on the one board with Flash Encryption already provisioned (the only board that can run the production HTTPS profile the route lives behind) blocks the route from ever being exercised live.

This remaining Wi-Fi issue ('Bug C' in this project's own memory) was extensively investigated and several specific hypotheses were tested and RULED OUT this round: MAC-address filtering on the user's own FRITZ!Box router (confirmed set to 'allow all new wireless devices'), corruption of the phy_init RF-calibration partition from an earlier-session flash-erase action (re-erased and forced a fresh recalibration -- no change, and the 100% deterministic, zero-variance failure pattern across 11 identical retries argues against a marginal-calibration-quality explanation anyway), and an ESP-IDF 5.5.2-vs-5.5.5 toolchain regression (an earlier finding from before Bugs D/E were fixed claimed 5.5.2 connects reliably; re-tested this round with the current, fixed code on both toolchains -- both now fail identically, 0/19 and 0/16 real connections respectively, directly contradicting and superseding that earlier claim).

The one remaining, untested hypothesis is that Flash Encryption itself (or something in its Development-mode runtime behavior specific to this exact device) is the real differentiator -- the third board (no Flash Encryption) connects at 100% reliability on the same network with the same code. This could not be tested directly: Flash Encryption Development mode is enforced at the eFuse/bootloader level once burned, independent of sdkconfig, and cannot be 'turned off' for a clean A/B test without either burning more eFuse changes (out of scope -- the user's own instruction was not to touch eFuse on the working board) or consuming the device's last remaining 'plaintext flash' allowance for a test that would just get silently re-encrypted by the bootloader anyway (the user's own explicit call, given via AskUserQuestion, was to stop here rather than spend that one-time allowance).

bug_c_resolution.status: ROOT-CAUSED AND FIXED, verified on real hardware
bug_c_resolution.correction_notice: This supersedes the 'honest_scope_boundary' text above, which was written while Bug C was still open and named Flash Encryption as the leading untested hypothesis. Flash Encryption was a red herring: it mattered only because it shrinks the heap budget, which made an ALREADY-PRESENT memory bug cross a threshold. The same latent bug exists on every profile.
bug_c_resolution.root_cause: Four global objects in main/app_main.cpp held ~166KB of permanently reserved .bss: g_mqtt (MqttBridge, 101692 bytes), g_runtime (ServiceRuntime, 41240), g_registry (CoreRegistry, 20624), g_matter (MatterBridge, 6808 .data). The dominant single contributor was MqttBridge's `pending_publications_[192]` staging queue -- 192 x sizeof(MqttPublishedMessage) (64-byte topic + 384-byte payload + flag = 452) = ~85KB, reserved for the device's entire uptime even though the queue is purely transient (filled by one sync pass, then drained to empty in batches of 8 in the same task iteration). On the production + Flash-Encryption profile this left the Wi-Fi driver with almost no DMA-capable heap during association: measured directly on hardware at the moment of disconnect, freeDMA was 280-476 bytes with a largest free block of 92-272 bytes.
bug_c_resolution.how_found: Systematic differential diagnosis against a known-good board, then direct measurement. (1) Line-by-line boot-log diff between the failing board and a working one isolated ESP-IDF coexistence (`coexist: coex firmware version`, present on 16/16 failing boots, 0/N working boots) as the one consistent difference. (2) Disabling CONFIG_ESP_COEX_SW_COEXIST_ENABLE made the auth stage pass immediately (init -> auth -> assoc -> run, RSSI -59, SNR 38) but moved the failure to a WPA2 4-way-handshake timeout (reason=15), proving the problem was not RF arbitration and not signal. (3) A temporary heap probe added to the STA-disconnected event handler measured the DMA-capable heap at the exact failure moment, revealing near-total exhaustion. (4) `idf.py size-components` plus a parse of the .map file's largest .bss symbols identified the four global objects and pinned MqttBridge's queue as the dominant one. (5) Temporarily shrinking the queue to 16 entries took the same board from 0/19 connections to 11/11 with zero disconnects, confirming causality before any permanent change was written.
bug_c_resolution.unified_explanation: This single cause explains what had been tracked as three separate bugs. The Wi-Fi driver's `m f auth`, `m f assoc req` and `m f beacon` messages are frame-buffer allocation failures (the driver prints the explicit form, `alloc eb len=752 type=4 fail`, on the SoftAP path). Bug B (SoftAP crash) and Bug C (STA auth timeout) were the same heap exhaustion failing at whichever stage happened to allocate first; coexistence, which needs its own memory, simply consumed enough extra to push the failure earlier (auth instead of the 4-way handshake). This also explains every previously puzzling property: 100% deterministic (memory exhaustion is deterministic), unaffected by signal strength or distance, unaffected by router MAC filtering, unaffected by phy_init/RF calibration, and unaffected by ESP-IDF toolchain version.
fixes_applied: components/mqtt_bridge: `pending_publications_` changed from a plain member array to a lifecycle-scoped allocation (new `ensure_publication_queue()`/`release_publication_queue()`), claimed in MqttBridge::start() -- which runs only once the network is already up, i.e. exactly when the Wi-Fi association buffers are no longer needed -- and released in stop(), after the worker task has exited. Capacity (192) and drop-when-full semantics are unchanged; the existing capacity guards now compare against a `pending_publication_capacity_` member that is 0 when unallocated, so a failed allocation degrades to skipping publications rather than misbehaving. Allocation is also attempted lazily from the two staging paths, which keeps every existing host test working unchanged (many call sync_snapshot() without start()).

components/service/persisted_state_store.cpp: `probe_slot()`'s ~2.2KB `WireRecord` stack local moved to function-local `static`. save() calls probe_slot() twice while its own WireRecord-sized scratch is already live in its frame, putting ~4.5KB on the stack at once; this really did overflow the service_runtime task (a 'Stack protection fault' resolving to exactly this function) on the network-up persistence path, which only became reachable once Wi-Fi association started working. Same reasoning and same fix already applied in load() and state_persistence_coordinator.cpp.

components/service/service_runtime.cpp: kRuntimeTaskStackSize returned to 16384 (from the 11264 that Bug F had forced). With ~85KB of .bss freed, this profile now boots with ~148KB of heap instead of ~66KB, so a stack with real margin over the deepest measured path (~12.5KB) is affordable again instead of sitting ~1KB under a ceiling.
bug_c_resolution.verification_on_real_hardware: Final build: production profile + Flash Encryption (Development mode) + coexistence RE-ENABLED (i.e. Zigbee 802.15.4 arbitration active, the configuration the product actually needs), flashed to the same board that had failed 0/19. Result over a 55-second capture window: 1 boot and no reboots at all (previously the board crash-looped 10-16 times per window), coex firmware loaded, Wi-Fi connected, DHCP IP 192.168.11.164 obtained, ZERO disconnects, ZERO crashes, mDNS advertising https://zigbee-gateway-9f0020.local, and the production HTTPS listener correctly failing closed on 'active-slot certificate unavailable' (its TLS material was wiped by an earlier, unrelated NVS erase this session -- the fail-closed gate behaving exactly as designed). Heap at boot: 148 KiB, up from 66 KiB.
bug_c_resolution.checks: 109/109 host tests passing (unchanged count -- the lazy-allocation path keeps every existing MqttBridge test working without modification), cppcheck clean on all three changed files (only pre-existing style findings remain), check_arch_invariants.sh high=0/medium=0/low=0 (confirming components/mqtt_bridge has no heap-allocation prohibition, unlike components/matter_bridge under INV-M040 or core/service under INV-H002), real idf.py build clean on the production + Flash-Encryption profile.
bug_c_resolution.postmortem_document: docs/process/POSTMORTEM_WIFI_HEAP_STARVATION.md -- standalone engineering post-mortem: the full symptom set, the `m f <frame>` = malloc-failed decoding insight that unified three apparently separate bugs, the memory attribution table, every hypothesis tested and ruled out (signal, MAC filtering, antenna, phy_init/RF calibration, ESP-IDF 5.5.2-vs-5.5.5, project Zigbee/OTA contention, Flash Encryption, coexistence), the five-step diagnostic method, all three fixes with their rationale, and the reusable lessons.

tls_identity_reprovisioning.status: DONE and verified on real hardware
tls_identity_reprovisioning.why: This board's TLS identity material was wiped by a flash erase performed earlier in this same investigation, so start_production_https() was failing closed on 'active-slot certificate unavailable' -- the last thing standing between a stable device and a reachable certificate-rotation route.
tls_identity_reprovisioning.what_was_generated: A fresh private product CA and device leaf certificate via real openssl: EC P-256, 7300 days, chain verified with `openssl verify`, carrying exactly the two SAN values this device's own validator requires -- DNS:zigbee-gateway-9f0020.local and URI:urn:zgw:98a3169f0020 (derived from the real factory base MAC 98:a3:16:9f:00:20). All three PEMs are well under the kTlsCertOrKeyMaxBytes (4096) storage bound.
tls_identity_reprovisioning.method: A temporary block in app_main() ahead of g_web_server.start(), exercising S5 #13's real storage port directly: service::tls_identity_set_product_ca(), _set_certificate(TlsCertificateSlot::kCurrent, ...), _set_private_key(...). Lengths passed as sizeof() rather than strlen() so each PEM's trailing NUL is stored -- mbedtls requires it, and this project's own rotation route explicitly rejects its absence.
tls_identity_reprovisioning.verification: Two flashes. (1) With the provisioning block: all three writes returned success, `hal_nvs: set_blob ok, key='tls_cert_cur' len=819`, `secure_storage: wrote key='tls_cert_cur' value=[REDACTED 819 bytes]`, and the production listener came up -- `esp_https_server: Server listening on port 443` -- meaning the real validator accepted the chain and both SANs. (2) The block and its data header were then removed via targeted Edit (never git checkout, per this project's own hard-won lesson about that file) and a clean rebuild produced a byte-identical binary size to the pre-hook build, confirming the removal was exact; reflashed, the device read tls_cert_cur / tls_key_cur / tls_ca back from encrypted NVS (all status=0) and again reached `Server listening on port 443`, with tls_active_state absent (status=1) so cert_rotation_state correctly defaulted to kCurrent/confirmed. One boot, no reboots, zero crashes, zero Wi-Fi disconnects across the capture window.
tls_identity_reprovisioning.key_material_location: Preserved outside the repository at ~/zigbee-gateway-hil-tls/ (ca_cert.pem, ca_key.pem, device_cert.pem, device_key.pem, ext.cnf, README.txt). Deliberately not committed -- these are real private keys. ca_key.pem is retained specifically because issuing a NEW leaf signed by the same CA is exactly what exercising the rotation route requires.

unresolved_blockers: The certificate-rotation route (S6 #12/FD-17) still has no live HIL exercise, but every device-side precondition is now met: the board boots stably with working Wi-Fi under the production profile and serves HTTPS on port 443 from persisted encrypted TLS material. What remains is purely a matter of driving a real request at it, which needs (a) network reachability -- on the extender SSID the board lands on the extender's own subnet (192.168.11.x) and is not reachable from this WSL2 environment, so the request must come from the Windows host, another device on that segment, or the board must join the main router's SSID -- and (b) a real physical button press by the user to mint the physical-presence grant the route requires.
releaseability: The four bugs in this file are real, independently verified fixes with no known regressions (all re-tested on both the production+Flash-Encryption profile and the plain development profile after the Bug F correction). They represent genuine hardening of this project's boot-time task/stack management, found only by real hardware HIL testing, and are releasable on their own merits regardless of Bug C's outcome. Certificate rotation's own live HIL exercise remains the one item this whole investigative thread set out to reach and did not; it is deferred pending either a resolution to Bug C or a decision to accept a different board/profile combination for that specific test. No live production deployment yet (see memory project-not-yet-in-production.md).
